Speaker script

Two-layer survival-aware CAR-T scheduling

1 The framework

This is the framework. There are two layers. The top one is strategic: a network-design model that decides which facilities to open, capacity, patient-to-facility assignment, and transport. The new part is that when manufacturing starts becomes a decision, not fixed to the day material arrives, so there's a real queue, and patient survival enters the objective through a tier-specific decay curve. That's solved once and frozen. The bottom layer runs on that frozen network. It's a daily simulation: patients arrive and deteriorate while they wait, and manufacturing batches either pass or fail release testing. Every time a slot frees, a small look-ahead optimization re-decides who to start next, based on the state it actually observes that day. And if a batch fails, the patient needs a fresh collection, which we only allow if their projected survival at the eventual delivery still clears a floor; otherwise they're cancelled. So the whole thing reacts to failure as it happens.

2 The policies 45 sec

[point to the “Policies compared” box]

At that decision point I compare five policies, and they differ only in who they pick to manufacture next:

  • FIFO — serve in arrival order, ignoring health. That's my do-nothing baseline.
  • Survival index — a simple closed-form rule: serve whoever loses the most survival from one more day of waiting. No solver needed.
  • Static survival — optimize the whole schedule once up front, then just follow it, never re-solving.
  • Adaptive MPC — the full version: re-optimize at every epoch on the state it actually observes. This is the one I'm proposing.
  • Perfect-information bound — not a real policy, but the best schedule if you knew every failure in advance. It's the ceiling I measure everyone against.

The nice thing is the comparison isolates two things cleanly: FIFO versus the survival-aware ones shows the value of caring about survival at all, and static versus adaptive shows the value of re-optimizing as failures unfold.

3 Measures and the insight 1 min — keep it light

I won't go deep into results today, but just so you know what I'm measuring: high-risk patients lost, total lost, cost, hold time by tier, and how close I get to that perfect-information benchmark. The headline is that the schedule reorders who waits so the sickest move to the front, and, importantly, that's emergent: there's no priority rule in the model; it falls out of the survival calibration. And the value shows up under stress: when the system is congested, or failures are frequent, re-optimizing dynamically pulls away from a fixed schedule. The most defensible version of the story is that the benefit is operational: it comes from scheduling, not from redesigning the network.

Anticipated questions

Q1 · Why are the waiting (hold) days not integers?

One sentence: any individual patient waits a whole number of days; the fractional numbers you're showing are averages.

Detail: hold time is reported as the mean hold by tier, averaged over all patients in that tier and over the 30 random-yield replications. An average of integers is almost never an integer. Same point applies to “expected patients lost” — that's a probability sum (an expected value), so it's continuous by construction, not a headcount. So if he points at “2.9 days” or “4.8 patients,” the honest answer is: those are expectations across patients and seeds, not a single patient's experience. Nothing in the model uses fractional days — every duration in the network is integer, which is exactly why the survival linearization is exact.

Q2 · Why are MPC and the survival index so similar?

One sentence: the index rule is exactly the special case of the MPC problem when one slot frees at a time and you don't look ahead, and in these instances looking ahead almost never changes the immediate pick — so they nearly coincide.

Detail: the per-epoch MPC minimizes weighted survival loss over a look-ahead window with a continuation value for deferral. When a single slot frees — the common case here — and the survival curves are smooth and monotone, the optimal immediate start is just the patient with the largest priority-weighted one-day survival loss, which is the index. The look-ahead and the capacity coupling only change the answer when several slots and patients interact tightly, which is rare in these instances.

Frame it as a feature: it's a deployability result — a solver-free, clinician-inspectable rule captures almost all the value of the full optimization. But be ready for the sharper follow-up, “then why claim MPC at all?” Answer: MPC is the general, principled object; the index is its closed form under the simple case, and the empirical near-match is itself a finding, not an assumption. They separate under heavier congestion and failure, where the coupling bites — so you report MPC as the policy and the index as the interpretable approximation that happens to track it here.

Q3 · What exactly is “patient load,” and how is it computed?

One sentence: offered load is demand over capacity — how many patients want a manufacturing slot per day relative to how many the network can actually start per day.

Detail: capacity in starts per day is the total concurrent slots divided by the manufacturing lead time, since each slot is tied up for T_MFE = 7 days (so 14 slots → 14/7 = 2.0 starts/day). Demand is the arrival rate, patients per day across the arrival window. Load is the ratio; at the operating point (N = 200 on m1+m3) that's roughly 2.27 arrivals/day ÷ 2.0 starts/day ≈ 1.14. In Experiment B you vary load by compressing or expanding the arrival window on the fixed network — squeezing the same patients into fewer days raises arrivals per day, hence load — so load moves without changing the network or confounding the comparison. Load above 1 means demand outruns throughput, a queue forms, and that's precisely the regime where who-you-serve-first starts to matter.
